claims.text: Conventional processing of refractory high-entropy alloys yields homogeneous microstructures through mechanisms such as uniform grain refinement or precipitation hardening.
Data-driven or machine-learning optimization of thermo-mechanical processing parameters can induce tailored graded microstructures in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed processing can control gradients in grain size, lamellar spacing, and phase distribution.
The approach is intended to operate at ambient and moderately elevated temperatures relevant to structural applications.
The resulting microstructure contains spatially interlaced fine, high-strength regions and coarser, ductile regions.
Higher-strength regions in the heterogeneous microstructure bear a significant portion of the applied load.
Adjacent ductile regions accommodate plastic deformation and produce strain partitioning.
Engineered microstructural heterogeneity delays premature crack initiation.
Engineered microstructural heterogeneity delays crack propagation.
Strain partitioning between strong and ductile regions overcomes the strength-ductility trade-off.
The optimized graded refractory high-entropy alloy will have higher yield strength than its conventionally processed homogeneous counterpart.
The optimized graded refractory high-entropy alloy will have greater tensile ductility than its conventionally processed homogeneous counterpart.
Conventionally processed refractory high-entropy alloys typically gain strength at the expense of ductility.
Insufficient precision in controlling the microstructural gradient could prevent the desired property improvements.
Alloy-specific phase-stability problems could limit the success of the proposed approach.
Poor-quality data supplied to the optimization procedure could undermine the desired property improvements.
